PG-02 · Storage

PostgreSQL Physical Storage Internals

How a logical relation becomes forks, files, 8 KB pages, line pointers and tuple versions — plus TOAST, visibility maps, and what TRUNCATE really changes.

Validated on PostgreSQL 18.6
Core model. A table is a logical relation identified by an OID. Its current physical storage is identified by a filenode. That storage is split into forks, optionally into segment files, and then into fixed-size pages containing line pointers and tuples.

1. From relation to page

Relation / OID→Filenode→Fork→Segment file→8 KB page→Line pointer→Tuple
ConceptPostgreSQLMySQL / InnoDBMongoDB / WiredTiger
Default page size8 KB16 KBDifferent storage model; not a direct equivalent
Large valuesTOAST, potentially out-of-lineLarge columns can use off-page storageVariable-length document storage managed by WiredTiger
Visibility helperVisibility MapNo direct simple equivalentNo direct simple equivalent
Important filesystem detail
base/16393 is the database directory. 16453 is a relation file, not another directory. So inspect it with ls -lh base/16393/16453*, not cd base/16393/16453.

2. Prove the page layout

SHOW block_size;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('heap_demo')) AS main_size,
       pg_relation_size('heap_demo')
       / current_setting('block_size')::int AS pages;
 block_size
------------
 8192

 main_size | pages
-----------+------
 96 kB     | 12

The relation is exactly 12 default-size pages: 12 × 8192 = 98304 bytes = 96 KiB.

SELECT *
FROM page_header(get_raw_page('heap_demo', 0));
 lower | upper | special | pagesize
-------+-------+---------+---------
    92 |  1936 |    8192 |    8192
Page header
24 bytes.
Line pointers
lower = 92 means 68 bytes follow the header, enough for 17 four-byte item identifiers.
Free space
The raw free region is between lower and upper. The FSM reports a quantized approximation rather than an exact byte count.
Tuple area
Tuples grow backward from the upper end of the page.
SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_len, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('heap_demo', 0))
LIMIT 15;
 lp | lp_off | lp_len | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |   7824 |    364 |    770 |      0 | (0,1)
  2 |   7456 |    364 |    770 |      0 | (0,2)
 ...
 15 |   2672 |    364 |    770 |      0 | (0,15)
What CTID means
(0,1) means block 0, line pointer 1. The SQL-visible CTID matched the item identifier reported directly from page 0.

3. UPDATE creates a new tuple version

SELECT id, ctid
FROM heap_demo
WHERE id = 1;
 id | ctid
----+------
  1 | (0,1)
UPDATE heap_demo
SET payload = payload || '-changed'
WHERE id = 1;

SELECT id, ctid, payload
FROM heap_demo
WHERE id = 1;
 id |  ctid  | payload
----+--------+---------------
  1 | (0,18) | row-1-changed

PostgreSQL did not overwrite the existing tuple in place. It created a new row version. The new version remained on block 0 but used a new line pointer, so the CTID changed from (0,1) to (0,18).

Why the same page?
The table was created with fillfactor = 80, leaving room for updates. This result is consistent with PostgreSQL placing the new tuple on the same page. It is also a good bridge into HOT and MVCC, but CTID alone is not enough to prove that this specific update was HOT.

4. FSM and Visibility Map

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('heap_demo','main')) AS main,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('heap_demo','fsm'))  AS fsm,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('heap_demo','vm'))   AS vm;
 main  |  fsm  |   vm
-------+-------+---------
 96 kB | 24 kB | 0 bytes
SELECT *
FROM pg_freespace('heap_demo')
LIMIT 15;
 blkno | avail
-------+------
     0 | 1824
     1 | 1824
 ...
    10 | 1824
    11 |    0

The FSM records how much space PostgreSQL believes is available on each page. It is designed for locating pages with enough free room, not for reporting exact byte-for-byte page free space.

SELECT * FROM pg_visibility_map_summary('heap_demo');
 all_visible | all_frozen
-------------+-----------
           0 |          0
VACUUM heap_demo;

SELECT * FROM pg_visibility_map_summary('heap_demo');
 all_visible | all_frozen
-------------+-----------
          12 |          0
What changed
After VACUUM, all 12 heap pages became marked all-visible. all_frozen remained 0 because the tuples did not need to be frozen. Visibility-map bits are set by VACUUM and cleared by data-changing operations on a page.

5. TOAST: 128 KB value, 8 KB main heap

SELECT octet_length(payload) AS logical_bytes,
       pg_column_size(payload) AS stored_datum_size,
       pg_column_compression(payload) AS compression,
       pg_column_toast_chunk_id(payload) AS toast_chunk_id
FROM toast_demo;
 logical_bytes | stored_datum_size | compression | toast_chunk_id
---------------+-------------------+-------------+---------------
        128000 |            128000 |             |         16465
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('toast_demo')) AS main_heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(
         (SELECT reltoastrelid
          FROM pg_class
          WHERE oid = 'toast_demo'::regclass)
       )) AS toast_total;
 main_heap  | toast_total
------------+------------
 8192 bytes | 176 kB

The non-NULL toast_chunk_id proves the value is stored out-of-line in the TOAST relation. compression is NULL, so this specific value was not compressed. The 128 KB value therefore lives primarily in TOAST storage even though the main heap itself occupies only one 8 KB page.

Why is TOAST 176 kB instead of exactly 128 kB?
TOAST storage also needs tuple headers, chunk-row overhead, page overhead, alignment, and a TOAST index. The physical footprint is therefore larger than the raw payload.

6. OID vs filenode: the TRUNCATE proof

SELECT 'heap_demo'::regclass::oid AS oid,
       pg_relation_filenode('heap_demo') AS filenode,
       pg_relation_filepath('heap_demo') AS filepath;
  oid  | filenode | filepath
-------+----------+------------------
 16453 |    16453 | base/16393/16453
TRUNCATE heap_demo;
  oid  | filenode | filepath
-------+----------+------------------
 16453 |    16466 | base/16393/16466
Logical identity
The OID stayed 16453. PostgreSQL still considers this the same relation object in the catalogs.
Physical identity
The filenode changed to 16466. TRUNCATE replaced the table's physical storage instead of deleting its rows one by one.

This is the precise lesson: OID and filenode are different kinds of identity. They may initially have the same number, but operations such as TRUNCATE, REINDEX, CLUSTER, and some forms of ALTER TABLE can assign new physical storage while preserving the logical relation OID.

7. Key takeaways

A heap is an array of pages.
Your 96 KiB relation consisted of 12 default 8 KiB pages.
CTID is physical.
An UPDATE changed the visible row location from (0,1) to (0,18).
FSM and VM have different jobs.
FSM tracks free-space availability; VM tracks all-visible/all-frozen page state.
TOAST is secondary storage.
A 128 KB text value lived out-of-line while the main heap remained only 8 KB.
OID ≠ filenode.
TRUNCATE preserved OID 16453 but moved physical storage to filenode 16466.
Logical and physical views are connected, not identical.
The catalogs identify objects; filenodes and pages implement their current storage.
